爱 takes things as well as people. 我爱吃辣 (I love spicy food) and 我爱这个地方 are ordinary, so hearing 爱 does not by itself signal romance — what signals it is the object being 你.
Chinese does not change the verb for the subject or the object, so 我爱你 is the same sentence whoever says it. 'I love you too' is therefore 我也爱你, with 也 before 爱.

when: At a table when the glasses come together: the same two words work as the invitation to drink and as the answer to one.
Not only formal dinners. It is the ordinary toast among friends, colleagues and family, and you will hear it several times in an evening.

variants.note: The short form of the same word. Very common at lively tables and it means exactly the same thing.

variants.en: I will finish mine, you drink as you like.
variants.note: The polite way to toast somebody who may not want to match you glass for glass.
敬 is the verb for toasting a person, used to a host, an elder or a guest of honour.

mistakes: 干杯 means empty the glass, not clink and sip. If you are not drinking alcohol, 我以茶代酒 (I will drink tea instead) is understood and accepted, and your glass stops being refilled.
There is an order to it. The host toasts first, and when a younger person toasts somebody older the glass is held slightly lower. Getting that right matters more than the word.
Toasting here is social rather than competitive. 随意 (as you like) is the standard escape hatch, and saying it once protects you for the rest of the evening.

when: To anyone on their birthday — a friend, a colleague, someone at the next table.
Very often written rather than spoken: on a card, on a red envelope, or in a chat message.

variants.note: The fuller form. 祝 is the verb 'to wish', so this reads as a formal wish rather than a shout.
Common with older people, where a wish for health carries more weight than the birthday itself.
The 啊 at the end makes it sound spoken and warm rather than read off a card.

mistakes: 生日快乐 is only for birthdays. The formula is occasion + 快乐: 新年快乐 (Happy New Year), 节日快乐 (happy holiday), 周末快乐 (have a good weekend). 快乐 always comes second.
It is said on the day, not in advance — there is no Chinese equivalent of 'many happy returns'.
The short version is the common one. Adding 祝你 makes it warmer in writing, not more correct in speech.

when: You say it as the answer to 对不起, and when somebody apologises for a small accident — bumping into you, stepping on your foot, knocking your bag.
It also closes a problem rather than accepting an apology: it says the whole thing has stopped mattering, so use it to end a complaint rather than to open one.

variants.note: The short everyday version, used constantly in speech. Fine after a bump in a crowd; too light for an apology that was meant seriously.
The warmer twin of 没关系. 要紧 means 'to matter', so 不要紧 is 'it doesn't matter' — you will hear staff use it to wave off an apology.
For something the other person feels genuinely bad about. 放在心上 is literally 'put it in your heart', so this is the phrase that actually forgives.

mistakes: It answers 对不起, not 谢谢. Reply to thanks with 不客气 — 没关系 after 谢谢 sounds as though you are forgiving the person rather than accepting their gratitude.
It dismisses the incident, not the person's feeling. If you want to say 'no harm done, but please be careful', 没关系 will not carry it, because it closes the topic.
Tone decides whether it lands. A flat 没关系 after a real apology reads as cold; the same words with 真 in front (真没关系) are what make the other person believe you.

replies.en: I'll be on my way then.

when: Say it when you need a few seconds — to find the word you want, to open a payment app, or to check the change. 请 in front keeps it a request and 一下 keeps it short.
It is the phrase for someone who is mid-task: a cashier ringing up your basket, a clerk already serving another customer, a driver stopped at a light.

variants.note: Drop the 请 and this is what friends and colleagues say to each other all day. To a stranger it can land as abrupt, so keep the 请 there.
The service-counter version. 稍 is the 稍 of 稍微 (slightly); you will hear it in shops, banks and on customer-service lines.
Buying time for a decision rather than for a task. The doubled 想想 makes it "think a little", which is softer than a flat 想.

mistakes: 等一下 is not rude on its own — tone carries it. Said flatly to a stranger it reads as an order; with 请 in front it is a request.
等一下 points at the task, not at you. To mean "wait for me" while you are the one walking ahead, Chinese says 等我一下 — 等我 (wait for me) plus 一下.
一 changes tone here: it is yī standing alone but yí before a fourth tone like xià. The same shift gives 一个 (yí ge) and 一次 (yí cì).

when: Say it to turn down something that is being offered — a tout at a station exit, a driver quoting a fare, an assistant holding up a second item.
The 谢谢 on the end matters more than it looks: it marks the refusal as a decision about the offer rather than a judgement about the person, and it gives them a clean place to stop.

variants.note: Flatter and more final than 不用了. In a crowd it is the one that ends the exchange fastest.
Turns the refusal into a fact about you rather than a verdict on the offer — useful when the same person asks a second and third time.
A soft brush-off for the second or third ask. 吧 makes it a suggestion rather than a closed door, which suits a street you might walk down again.

mistakes: 不用 is not a word-for-word "no thanks": 用 is "to need", so 不用 is "not needed". The literal sense is firmer than the English sounds, and the 谢谢 is what keeps it polite.
Chinese has no single word for "no". A flat 不 on its own sounds like a challenge; refusals come as 不用了, 不要了 or 不行, one situation at a time.
The 了 in 不用了 is doing work: it marks a decision being made now. 不用 without it can read as a general statement — "not needed" — rather than a reply to the offer in front of you.

replies.en: Come find me if you need anything.

when: Use it the moment you are introduced to someone — right after the handshake or the nod — as the standard way to open a new acquaintance in Chinese.
It also fits hosts, guides, hotel managers and a friend's parents, though people of your own age usually just say 你好 again and get straight to talking.

variants.note: The same words with the feeling first — this is the order you will hear most often.
Short and slightly formal; it belongs to exchanged business cards rather than parties.
见到 is about the meeting itself, so it fits the moment you go from messages to face to face.

mistakes: Not for service staff. You are not introduced to a waiter or a cashier, so 认识你很高兴 lands as oddly weighty there — a plain 你好 is what people actually say.
认识 is for people, 知道 is for facts. 我知道你 means "I know of you", which is a very different thing to say to someone you have just met.
幸会 does not mix with 很高兴. Pick one register and stay in it: 幸会幸会 for a card exchange, 很高兴认识你 for everybody else.

when: Say it early in a conversation you are struggling through. It reframes the whole exchange: once the person knows you are a visitor, they stop testing whether you understood and start explaining instead.
It is also the sentence that opens the door for help — knowing you do not know the local routine makes a follow-up question expected rather than an imposition.

variants.note: Works in the same places as 我是游客 but carries no holiday context — useful at a bank, a clinic or anywhere a clerk is deciding how much to explain.
刚 marks "only just". Adding it explains why you have no local number, no payment app set up and no idea of the routine yet.

variants.en: This is my first time here.
variants.note: The one that reliably gets patience and invites recommendations. 第一次 is the frame for any first time — 第一次来中国, 第一次吃火锅.

mistakes: 游客 means a sightseeing visitor. A business traveller is 出差 (chūchāi) and a student is 留学生, so 我是游客 is the wrong label on a work trip.
Saying it is a strategy, not a confession. Staff change register when they hear it: instructions get repeated, and answers come with the extra step that a local would have been expected to know.
It is a label, not an apology, so no 不好意思 is needed. English adds "sorry, I'm just a tourist"; in Chinese the sorry makes it sound like you are apologising for being there.

when: You say it reacting to good news: a table found, a plan confirmed, a problem somebody else just solved. It is genuine enthusiasm, not politeness.
It is also how you praise something you were given or shown — a dish, a photo, somebody's Chinese — where a plain 很好 would sound flat.

variants.note: The plain version of the same frame, and the one you will hear most. 好 is safe anywhere; 棒 is louder and younger.
A little more measured than 太棒了. 不错 is 'not bad', and with 真 in front it turns into real praise.
For a person's skill or effort rather than a piece of news. 厉害 is the standard compliment for somebody who just did something difficult.

mistakes: 太…了 needs the 了. 太棒 on its own is not a sentence; the unit is 太 + adjective + 了, which covers 太好了, 太贵了 and 太辣了 alike.
太 means both 'so' and 'too much', and the adjective decides which. 太棒了 is praise while 太贵了 (too expensive) and 太辣了 (too spicy) are complaints — same frame, opposite job.
很棒 and 太棒了 do not sit in the same place. 很棒 describes something (this place is great); 太棒了 reacts to something (that's great!). Using 太棒了 as a description is what makes it sound over the top.

when: Only when someone is in real danger — a medical emergency, a fire, a serious accident, or harassment.
Shout it to draw the attention of anyone nearby. It is the one word that reliably stops people in a crowd.

variants.note: A request for help, but nowhere near as urgent as 救命. For being stuck, overloaded or lost rather than in danger.
The everyday request. Perfectly fine when you simply cannot manage on your own.
The follow-up that matters in a medical emergency.

mistakes: 救命 is not 'help me with this bag'. Spending it on a small problem wastes the one word that makes people act — for everything else use 帮忙 or 帮帮我.
Keep it for danger. A bystander who believes you are in danger may well call the police (110) on your behalf, which turns a small problem into a long one.
Emergency numbers in China: 110 police, 120 ambulance, 119 fire. Hotel staff and passers-by can also place the call for you.

replies.en: I'll call an ambulance for you.

when: When something has genuinely gone wrong: a lost passport, a stolen bag, or a phone that has died before you have anywhere to stay.
Say it to staff rather than to a passer-by. Hotel front desks, station service counters and shop assistants can make calls and check records, which strangers cannot.

variants.note: The direct question form. Works well straight after 不好意思 when you are already talking to somebody.
Much lighter, for a small immediate favour such as reading a sign or lifting a bag.

variants.en: I need to see a doctor.
variants.note: The same 我需要 frame carries any need: 我需要充电器 (a charger), 我需要一张地图 (a map).

mistakes: Do not reach for 救命 here. 救命 means somebody's life is in danger, and spending it on a lost phone empties the word for the moment it is really needed.
Name the person you need if you can. 前台 is the hotel front desk and 服务台 is the service counter in a station or a mall, so pointing at it plus 我需要帮助 covers the gap when the sentence runs out.
帮助 is the written and formal word. In speech people say 帮我, which is why 请帮我一下 sounds far more natural at a shop counter.

replies.py: Qǐng shāoděng, wǒ zhǎo gè rén.
replies.en: One moment, let me find someone.

when: You say it when something illegal has happened to you — a theft, a pickpocket, an assault, or a driver who will not settle after an accident.
Say it to hotel staff, a shop assistant or a station attendant rather than to a passer-by: they can place the call and can tell the operator where you are.

variants.note: The number by itself is an instruction, and every adult in China knows it. 一 is read yāo on the phone, so it carries over a noisy line.

variants.en: I want to report a crime.
variants.note: What you say once the call connects, or to a staff member who asks what you need. 报警 is the standard verb for calling the police.

variants.en: I need a copy of the police report.
variants.note: Ask for it before you leave the station. Travel insurers usually want written proof that a report was filed, and it is issued on the spot.

mistakes: 110 is the police, 120 the ambulance and 119 the fire service. Dialling the wrong one is not a disaster because the operators transfer you, but naming the right number gets you there faster.
On the phone 一 is read yāo, not yī. That is why 110 comes out as yāo-yāo-líng and 120 as yāo-èr-líng — and why a number shouted over traffic is still understood.
Police in China take identification from the person reporting. Carry your passport, and for anything involving a hotel room or an insured item keep the registration slip or the receipt with it.

when: A medical emergency where somebody cannot get to hospital on their own.
Say it to whoever is nearest. A clear instruction moves strangers to act far faster than a general cry for help.

variants.note: 快 in front is what makes it urgent. This is the version to shout across a street.
The number alone is an instruction. 120 is the ambulance line and everyone in China knows it.
Explains why you are asking, and gives whoever is listening something to act on.

mistakes: On the phone, 一 is read yāo and not yī. 120 is yāo-èr-líng, which is what makes the number clear over traffic noise.
An ambulance in China is not free: the ride is charged for separately from the hospital bill. Cost should not decide anything in a real emergency, but it is worth knowing this is a paid service.
If the person can walk, a taxi is usually faster. 医院在哪里 plus the nearest driver gets you there sooner than waiting for a crew, and the hospital 急诊 (emergency department) is open all night.

when: Say it while showing someone the Chinese name of your hotel on your phone — names and pictures get you found far faster than any spoken description.
迷路 means to lose your way, and 了 marks the change of state: you were fine a moment ago, and now you are lost.

variants.note: 走丢 is the everyday word for someone who drifted away from their group — also what parents shout about children in a crowd.

variants.en: I want to go back to my hotel.
variants.note: Swap in your hotel's name — 我要回香格里拉 works the same way and names the destination in one go.
Point at the ground under your feet — it makes any local open their map app for you.

mistakes: 迷路 means you yourself are lost; 找不到 means you cannot find something you are looking for. You 迷路 on the street, but you 找不到 your hotel entrance even on a street you know.

Street names in China often change along one road, and building numbers restart at each crossing — directions by address numbers fail fast, so landmarks and shop-front photos beat any verbal description.
For a companion missing in a crowd, use 走丢 too: 我朋友走丢了 (my friend got lost) is understood instantly at any information desk — and loud enough to gather help.

replies.py: Bié jí, wǒ bāng nín kànkan.
replies.en: Don't worry, let me take a look.
Which hotel are you going to?

replies.py: Qiánmiàn lùkǒu yòu zhuǎn jiù dào le.
replies.en: Turn right at the crossing ahead and you are there.

when: When you need care yourself and can still move: a fever that will not break, a sprained ankle, a cut that needs stitches.
Ask a hotel front desk, a pharmacy or a taxi driver. The same question gets you a hospital name, a direction, or a ride.

variants.note: The better question when you have no idea how far it is. 附近 means nearby, and the answer may be a pharmacy instead.
For anything small, start here. Pharmacies are everywhere and the staff will point you to a hospital if the problem is beyond them.
Large Chinese hospitals are several buildings with departments split across them. 急诊 is the one that never closes.

mistakes: The 在哪里 frame takes any place, so learn it once: 药店 pharmacy, 派出所 local police station, 地铁站 metro station, 洗手间 washroom.

Go to a large hospital rather than a small clinic. The biggest hospitals in a city have an international clinic (国际部) used to foreign patients, and 三甲 on the sign is the shorthand for a top-tier hospital.
The emergency department is the right door at night or at a weekend. Registration comes first when you arrive, and the passport is what the desk asks for.

replies.en: Turn right at the junction ahead.

replies.py: Jiù zài zhè tiáo jiē shàng.

when: Say it at a hotel front desk or to anyone nearby when you feel unwell and need medical help rather than a pharmacy.
Chinese hospitals usually take a sudden illness straight into 急诊 (the emergency department), instead of asking you to book a clinic appointment first.

variants.note: 挂号 is the first step of every hospital visit — pay a small fee, get a number, then wait to be called.
A 诊所 handles small problems; a 医院 handles everything else.
The traveler's most common complaint, and the colloquial 拉肚子 is exactly what triage staff expect to hear.

mistakes: The patient 看医生 (sees the doctor) and the doctor 看病 (sees the illness) — the same 看 points both ways, and 我看病 said by a patient is understood as the same thing.
Registering (挂号) is not optional — skip the window and there is no number, and without a number no doctor will call you, however empty the waiting room looks.
A pharmacy (药店) is often the faster stop for minor problems, because pharmacists there recommend and sell medicine directly — more street corners have one than have a clinic.

replies.en: The emergency department is on the first floor.
Go and register over there first.

when: Say it before you order, not after, and name the thing with 对…过敏 — 我过敏 on its own leaves everyone guessing what you need to avoid.
It is the line that gets you a real answer: staff usually know what is in a dish, but the safest version is to show the allergen written in Chinese and confirm it before anything is cooked.

variants.note: Swap in 牛奶 (milk), 鸡蛋 (egg) or 坚果 (nuts) for the same frame. 海鲜 covers fish, prawns, crab and shellfish in one word.

variants.py: Wǒ chī le huì hěn nánshòu.
variants.en: It makes me very ill if I eat it.
variants.note: Some kitchens hear 过敏 as a preference. Saying what happens to you moves it into the safety column, and that is the part that changes how they cook.
The checkable question, and the one worth asking again at the table — 花生油 (peanut oil) is common in Chinese cooking and never appears in a dish name.

mistakes: Allergy is a known idea in China but not a routine one, so 过敏 on its own is often heard as a mild dislike. Adding what happens to you is what turns it into a kitchen instruction.
过敏 needs its target: 我对…过敏 is the frame. 我过敏 by itself is what you say to a doctor, not to someone taking your order.
The riskiest ingredient is the one missing from the name — peanut oil in a stir-fry, sesame paste in a sauce, shrimp paste in a broth. Naming the dish is not enough; name the ingredient.

replies.py: Nà gěi nín huàn yí ge.
replies.en: Then let me swap it for something else.

when: Use it before any dish is chosen — the moment you sit down or open the menu — because peanut oil is common in Chinese kitchens and peanuts hide in dishes that do not look nutty.
过敏 (allergic) is what makes it medical: it is stronger than 我不吃花生 (I don't eat peanuts), which staff will hear as a preference they can talk you out of.

variants.note: 不能 (cannot) beats 不 (don't) here — 不 sounds like a choice, 不能 sounds like a rule, and kitchens take rules more seriously.
Ask it per dish at the same time as you order it — blanket questions about the whole menu get vague answers.
花生油 (peanut oil) is the default frying oil in many kitchens, and 放 is the cooking verb for adding it — this targets the oil, not just whole peanuts.

mistakes: The general allergy phrase 我过敏 (I'm allergic) names no trigger and often gets nothing but a nod. Naming it — 花生, 海鲜 (seafood), 牛奶 (milk), 坚果 (nuts) — is what makes the kitchen act.
Peanuts hide under famous names: 宫保鸡丁 (Kung Pao Chicken) is cooked with peanuts, and so are many cold starters. Ask even for dishes that sound safely meaty.
No visible peanuts is not the same as peanut-free — peanut oil leaves no trace to see. 不放花生油 (no peanut oil) covers the oil, because 没有花生 alone only rules out the nuts themselves.

replies.en: There are some peanuts in it.

when: When you need somebody to understand that you are unwell right now — a hotel front desk, a pharmacy counter, or a colleague you have to cancel on.
Name the symptom straight after it, because 我生病了 on its own says only that something is wrong; 我发烧了 or 我头疼 is what gets a specific answer.

variants.note: The specific one that moves things fastest. A fever is what pharmacies and clinics act on, and it is worth saying before anything else.
Softer and vaguer than 生病了 — 不舒服 covers everything from a headache to an upset stomach without naming it.
我 plus a body part plus 疼 builds any ache: 肚子疼 (stomach), 嗓子疼 (throat), 牙疼 (tooth).

mistakes: Chinese usually names the symptom rather than the general state. The English 'I'm sick' is a complete answer; 我生病了 is a door-opener, and the next question will be 哪里不舒服？ — so have the body part ready.
了 marks a change, so 我生病了 means you were fine and now you are not. For something long-standing you drop it and say 我身体不好, and the two are not interchangeable.

药店 is where you buy medicine and 医院 is where you are treated. Saying 我要去医院 for a headache will be heard as an emergency, so point yourself at 药店 for anything you would fix with over-the-counter medicine.

replies.en: Do you need to go to a hospital?

replies.py: Duō hē rè shuǐ, zǎodiǎn xiūxi.
replies.en: Drink more hot water and get some rest.

when: Say it at a hotel front desk or a police station as soon as you notice, because the sentence starts two things at once: a report where you are, and a call to your own embassy.
丢 marks a loss that has already happened and 了 closes it, so 护照丢了 says the passport is gone rather than misplaced — while 我找不到护照了 says only that you cannot put your hands on it right now.

variants.py: Wǒ de hùzhào bú jiàn le.
variants.note: Softer than 丢了 — the right first sentence in a hotel room, where it may still turn up.

variants.py: Wǒ zhǎo bú dào hùzhào le.

variants.en: I need to replace my passport.
variants.note: 补办 is the word for reissuing a lost document, and it is the one the paperwork is filed under.

mistakes: 丢了 and 不见了 both say the passport is not with you, but 不见了 leaves room for it turning up — at a hotel it is worth starting there and treating it as lost only after the room has been searched.
身份证 is the document Chinese nationals carry and 护照 is the one you carry, so keeping to 护照 keeps the questions away from an ID you will never have.
The passport number and a photo of the data page are what speed up the replacement: with them, 这是我的护照号码 gets the paperwork moving; without them, the process starts back at proving who you are.

replies.en: Which room are you staying in?
Please file a report at the local police station.

when: Use it at the hotel desk or police station right after noticing — a desk clerk making calls for you beats searching the streets alone.
It also turns bystanders from curious to helpful, since people respond to the news with action.

variants.py: Wǒ de bāo bèi tōu le.

mistakes: Saying 丢了 when you know it was stolen — 丢 means lost somewhere; 被偷 is the word police reports are built on.
Hunting the streets first — the fastest help is the nearest desk; hotel staff dial 110 and explain location faster than you can.
Delaying card cancellations — call the banks before the search; Chinese pickpockets move faster than tourists retrace steps.

replies.py: Bàojǐng le ma? Wǒ bāng nín dǎ.
replies.en: Have you called the police? I'll dial for you.
Keep the police report slip for replacing documents.

when: Use it for everyday medicine — pharmacies with green cross signs are everywhere and open until about 10 p.m.
The same question works for all-night branches, where a green cross with a 24-hour sign marks the exception.

variants.en: How do I get to the closest pharmacy?

mistakes: Assuming 24 hours — most close at 22:00; look for the 24小时 sign on the rare all-night branch.
Describing symptoms to strangers on the street — walk into the pharmacy itself; the pharmacist asks directly and triages honestly.
Expecting prescription rules like home — common painkillers are over the counter, but bring the original box if you carry daily medication.

replies.en: There's one at the intersection ahead.

replies.py: Mǎlù duìmiàn yǒu gè dà yàofáng.
replies.en: There's a big pharmacy across the street.
Five minutes' walk, on your right.

when: Use it before handing over anything — hotels, taxis, restaurants, markets; asking costs nothing and the tenth time saves an awkward minute.
It also covers metro gates and buses, where the app payment code works even when a counter has none.

variants.en: Can I scan this QR code?

mistakes: Opening the wrong app — 支付宝 and 微信支付 are rival wallets; vendors sometimes want one specifically and the other fails.
Arriving with an unlinked card — add your international card and test a tiny payment on day one, not at the checkout counter.
Asking where no code exists — metro gates and buses take app payment codes, so the question is only for counters and stalls.

replies.py: Nín sǎo wǒ, háishì wǒ sǎo nín?
replies.en: You scan mine, or I scan yours?

when: Use it at smaller vendors who run WeChat only because their regulars already live in the app, and as the fallback when an Alipay code errors out.
The same question is the natural fallback the moment the other wallet times out or errors twice.
mistakes: Funding only one wallet — top up and link cards in both apps; they fail at different moments and one saves the other.
Scanning a personal code when the official 商家码 errors — either can work, but ask which one when the first scan fails.
Skipping setup before the trip — WeChat Pay needs a linked card configured while you still have patience and Wi-Fi.

replies.en: Sure — scan my code with WeChat.

replies.zh: 微信有点问题，支付宝行吗？
replies.py: Wēixìn yǒudiǎn wèntí, Zhīfùbǎo xíng ma?
replies.en: WeChat is acting up — is Alipay okay?

when: Use it at any counter when you cannot tell how payment works here — no card reader in sight, no QR code propped up, and nobody has asked you for money yet.
The usual answer is 扫码 (sǎo mǎ, scan the code): either you scan their code with your phone, or they scan the code your app shows, and both directions are called the same thing.

variants.note: For markets and canteens where paying happens at a specific spot — this asks the place rather than the method.
收银台 is the cash register counter in shops and supermarkets — the landmark question when you are standing in the wrong aisle with an armful of goods.

variants.py: Kěyǐ sǎo nín de mǎ ma?
variants.note: Their printed code scanned by your app is one of the two QR directions; asking before pointing your camera keeps the moment friendly.

mistakes: 付款 and 付钱 are the shop verbs; restaurants have their own — 结账 (jiézhàng) or 买单 (mǎidān) is what you say when you want the bill, so in a restaurant the question becomes 怎么结账？

The two QR directions are easy to mix: scanning their code opens a payment page on your phone, while showing your code lets their scanner take money from you. If a staff member grabs your phone, they are doing the second one.
扣款 (kòukuǎn) on a banking app means an automatic deduction — it is not the counter word, and nobody says it when asking you to pay.

when: Say it as the bill arrives and you intend to be the one who pays. Reaching for the QR code while you say it is what makes it land, since the words alone can sound like an offer rather than a decision.
It is also what you say to a friend who is already holding a phone up to the scanner, because 来 means "let me do it" — 我来 claims the action instead of asking permission to do it.

variants.note: 次 counts occasions, so it leaves the next round to the other person.

variants.py: Nǐ lái diǎn, wǒ lái fù.
variants.note: The doubled 来 splits the two jobs neatly, and it settles things before the food even arrives.
转 is the verb for moving money in WeChat or Alipay, and it is the fallback when you are not next to the scanner.

mistakes: 付 is only about handing over money. 我来付 is about the bill, while 我来买 is about buying something, so swapping them turns "I'll pay" into "I'll buy this".
There is no single word that means splitting the bill. 我来付 claims the whole thing; to share it you say 我们 AA (spoken as the two English letters) or 各付各的 (gè fù gè de).
Expect to argue. The other person will say 我来我来 and mean it, and refusing twice before giving in is the script rather than a real conflict.

replies.py: Bù xíng bù xíng, wǒ lái.

when: When you are the one paying for everyone — a meal, a round of drinks, or the shared taxi at the end of the night.
Say it as you sit down or reach for the menu, because the offer to host is a claim you stake early rather than an answer you give when the bill arrives.

variants.note: 顿 is the measure word for meals, so 这顿 pins the treat to this one sitting rather than to a general habit.
算我的 claims the cost without the formal ring of 请客, which is useful when the other person is already reaching for their wallet.

variants.en: Don't stand on ceremony, it's on me.
variants.note: 别客气 is what you say when somebody pushes back. 我请 is 我请客 shortened, which is how it comes out in speech.

mistakes: 请客 is to host, not simply to pay. It carries the idea that you invited them, so announcing it after somebody else picked the restaurant can sound like you are taking over their occasion.

The first offer is usually waved away. Refusing once is the polite move rather than a real no, so 我请客 expects a second or third round before it settles — stopping after one refusal reads as not meaning it.
Do not translate 'split the bill' as 分钱. 分钱 is dividing money in general and can sound like haggling; 各付各的 or AA制 is the phrase for going Dutch.

replies.en: I can't let you do that!

when: Ask it at the till with a basket of things, or at the end of a meal when nobody has added anything up yet — 一共 is what turns a price question into a total question.
It comes just before payment, where 分开付 or 一起付 decides whether that total becomes several bills, so saying 一共 first is what makes the answer arrive as one number.

variants.en: What does it all come to?
variants.note: Literally "added up" — handy when the items are spread out on the counter.

variants.en: Please add it up for me.

mistakes: 多少钱 asks what one thing costs; 一共多少钱 is the sentence for a pile of things or a shared meal, and the two are not interchangeable at a till.
总共 and 一共 both mean "in total" and swap freely in speech, while 合计 is the word printed on receipts — which is why you read it more often than you hear it.
Some restaurants add a per-person 茶位费 or 餐位费 on top of what you ordered, so 还有别的费用吗 is the sentence that finds the gap between the menu prices and the number on the bill.

when: Use it when a group splits a bill — ask before anyone pays, then each person scans the table's code separately.
It also covers the coupon case, where one person pays with a deal and the others settle privately.

variants.py: Yì rén sǎo yí cì xíng ma?
variants.en: Can each of us scan once?

mistakes: Expecting a split-the-bill button — there is none at the table; AA happens by separate scans, one person per code.
Confusing AA制 with 各付各的 — AA splits the total evenly; 各付各的 means everyone pays for what they ordered.
Asking the waiter to divide — the kitchen brings one bill; the splitting happens at the QR step, not on paper.

replies.py: Kěyǐ, yì rén sǎo yí cì.
Wǒ xiān fù, nǐmen zhuǎn wǒ.
replies.en: I'll pay first, you all transfer me.

replies.py: Sǎo zhuō shàng de mǎ jiù xíng.
replies.en: Just scan the code on the table.

when: Use it when paying small cash amounts and the change is a few yuan — the local way for generosity to land without embarrassment.
The same sentence works for market stalls and small taxis alike, anywhere the change is small and the kindness is welcome.
mistakes: Waving off big change — 20 yuan on an 80 fare reads as confusion about the meter, not kindness.
Expecting service to transform — China has no tipping culture; this is politeness, and it lands as politeness.
Saying it during a fare dispute — settle the amount first; 不用找了 only means something when the number is agreed.

when: Use it when a company or insurer needs proof of purchase — 发票 is the official tax document, a different object from a till slip.
It also matters for insurance claims, where the official invoice is the only document that counts as proof.

variants.en: Put this as the invoice title.

mistakes: Confusing 发票 with 收据 — a 收据 is a mere receipt; reimbursement in China requires the tax-registered fapiao.
Giving the company title 抬头 by voice alone — carry it as text on your phone; one wrong character voids the document.
Expecting instant paper — many places email 电子发票; have an email address ready before you ask.

replies.en: Sure — let me have the invoice title.

when: Use it at the counter when your screen shows failure and the queue grows — the sentence explains everything and buys you patience.
The same sentence works when the code scans but errors, with the screen shown and the line said out loud.
mistakes: Struggling silently with the phone — staff see failed payments daily; showing the screen gets a second QR or a workaround in seconds.
Re-scanning ten times before asking — after two failures, say the sentence and hand the problem over.
Assuming your bank blocked it — usually it is the app's risk check on a new location; a retry after a minute often clears it.

replies.py: Bié jí, zài sǎo yí cì.

when: Use it when a foreign card declines — the default experience in China, since most terminals read UnionPay only.
It also sets up the graceful pivot to the payment app, which staff suggest the moment you say it.
mistakes: Retrying five times — foreign Visa and Mastercard rarely pass a POS terminal; two tries, then switch rails.
Blaming the merchant — their terminal genuinely cannot read the card; it is infrastructure, not attitude.
Forgetting bank ATMs — foreign cards usually DO work in bank machines for cash withdrawal, which is the reliable backup.

replies.py: Shuā bu liǎo guówài de kǎ.
replies.en: Foreign cards don't go through here.

replies.py: Nín yòng Zhīfùbǎo ba, dōu néng fù.
replies.en: Just use Alipay — it works everywhere.

when: You are ordering at a restaurant and want to rule out seafood in every dish — stir-fries, soups and dumplings all hide shrimp or shellfish in them.
It matters even more if your reaction is severe, and in that case follow it with 我对海鲜过敏 so the kitchen treats it as an allergy, not a taste.

variants.en: Don't put any seafood in it.

mistakes: Saying 不要辣 instead — that only covers chili heat, and a seafood-heavy dish with no spice at all will still land you in trouble.
Assuming broth is safe. Dried shrimp and seafood stock show up in vegetable dishes, so name the rule rather than pointing at the obvious dishes.
Whispering the sentence apologetically — kitchen staff need a clear rule, so say it at normal volume and repeat it once when the dish arrives.

replies.en: Sure, this dish has no seafood.
This one has shrimp in it.

when: You have stepped out of a station or hotel and want the metro instead of a taxi — in big cities the metro is faster than sitting in traffic at rush hour.
It works just as well for other transport hubs: swap 地铁站 for 汽车站 or 码头 and the sentence does not change shape.

variants.py: Zuìjìn de dìtiě zhàn zài nǎr?
variants.en: Where is the nearest metro station?
How do I get to the metro entrance?
Is there a metro around here?

mistakes: Dropping 站 and asking where the metro is — people will answer with the line name, not the entrance you can actually walk to.
Trusting the English signage all the way: exits are numbered in Chinese and pinyin only, so screenshot the exit letter your map app gives you.
Saving the question for lost moments only: asking at the hotel before you head out gets you a walking route instead of a rescue mission.

replies.py: Wǎng qián zǒu, hónglǜdēng yòu zhuǎn.
replies.en: Go straight ahead, turn right at the lights.

replies.py: Jiù zài qiánmiàn, dàgài wǔ fēnzhōng.
replies.en: It's just ahead, about five minutes.

when: You have reached the corner, gate or curb where the ride actually ends — drivers often keep going past the obvious spot out of habit.
It also stops the awkward meter run-up: say it with 前面 (further ahead) if traffic makes pulling over right away difficult.

variants.py: Shīfu, jiù zài zhèr tíng ba.

variants.en: Pull over to the side, please.

mistakes: Shouting the destination name again instead — the driver hears a place, not an instruction, and keeps driving while looking for it.
Arguing about the drop-off point after the meter stops: the fix is to say where to stop before the ride ends, not to renegotiate afterwards.
Waiting for the driver to notice the spot — from the road he cannot see the small alley you mean, so give the instruction before the landmark passes.

replies.en: Let's go a bit further ahead.

when: You are at the door of a museum, shop or scenic area and deciding whether to go in now or come back later.
Ticket offices at smaller sights often stop selling an hour before the site closes, so ask this before you queue — the same sentence with 开门 asks about opening.

variants.en: How late are you open today?

variants.py: Xiànzài hái jìn de qù ma?
variants.en: Can I still go in now?

mistakes: Reading closing times from a search result — holiday schedules change weekly at popular sights, and the ticket booth sign is the only truth.
Asking 关门吗 at the door — it sounds like you already assume the answer is no, and staff will just nod at you.
Pointing the question at a train station — stations stay open all day while the ticket windows shut, so aim it at sights and shops.

replies.py: Qī diǎn bàn jiù guānmén le.
replies.en: We close as early as seven thirty.

when: You are about to raise your phone in a temple, museum or border area where photography rules are stricter than they look.
Asking also works in your favour at markets and with street performers — many will pose happily or wave you closer once you have been polite.

variants.en: Is it OK to take photos?

variants.py: Wǒ néng gēn nǐ héyǐng ma?
variants.en: Can I take a photo with you?

mistakes: Mixing this up with the fitting-room sentence 我可以试试吗 — that one is for trying on clothes, and swapping them gets a puzzled laugh.
Shooting first at performances: the polite move is to ask, and to put the phone down immediately if someone waves you off.
Assuming one no covers the whole building — many places allow photos outside but never inside the main hall, so ask again at each threshold.

when: You have just checked in and the network card in the room is missing — the front desk keeps the password behind the counter and will read it out.
If the code is a long string of capitals and digits, follow up with 请写下来 and they will scribble it on the room card sleeve for you.

variants.en: Is there internet in the room?
I can't connect to the Wi-Fi.

mistakes: Pointing at your phone and smiling — staff will start a long explanation in Chinese when one set sentence gets you the code in five seconds.
Typing the password by ear: most hotel codes are case-sensitive, so ask the staff to type it into your phone directly instead of reading it out.
Trusting your memory for a 24-character code: even the staff retype it, so keep the card sleeve and take a photo of it as a backup.

replies.zh: 密码是大写 A 开头。
replies.en: The password starts with a capital A.

when: Your flight or train leaves in the evening and a noon checkout would strand you with your bags for hours.
Ask at the front desk the night before or at breakfast — hotels are far more flexible in the morning than at noon when the queue is forming.

variants.zh: 我可以下午两点退房吗？
variants.py: Wǒ kěyǐ xiàwǔ liǎng diǎn tuìfáng ma?
variants.en: Can I check out at two in the afternoon?

variants.zh: 行李可以寄存到晚上吗？
variants.py: Xínglǐ kěyǐ jìcún dào wǎnshang ma?
variants.en: Can my luggage stay until the evening?

variants.py: Wǎn tuìfáng yào jiā qián ma?
variants.en: Is there a charge for late checkout?

mistakes: Waiting until checkout time to ask — the answer at noon is almost always no, while a morning request often costs nothing at all.
Assuming late checkout is free everywhere: most hotels charge a half-day rate past a fixed hour, so ask about the fee before agreeing.
Mixing up late checkout with luggage storage — even when the room must be handed over at noon, bags almost always stay free at the desk.

replies.en: Leave your bags at the front desk first.

when: You have been kept up by street noise, thin walls or a late-night karaoke bar, and you want the hotel to fix it rather than endure it.
Front desks move guests before they admit a room is loud, so name the problem plainly and ask for another room in the same conversation.

variants.py: Néng gěi wǒ huàn ge fángjiān ma?
variants.en: Can you move me to another room?

variants.zh: 有没有安静一点的房间？
variants.py: Yǒu méiyǒu ānjìng yìdiǎn de fángjiān?
variants.en: Do you have a quieter room?

mistakes: Suffering through the night because you already checked in — Chinese hotels reassign rooms routinely, and asking at ten in the evening still works.
Explaining the noise in English at the desk: they act on what they can log, so give them the sentence plus your room number.
Making the request vague (a little noisy) — desks prioritise problems they can log, so name the source and ask for the room change outright.

replies.py: Gěi nín huàn dào bā lóu.
replies.en: We'll move you to the eighth floor.
There are no spare rooms now.
We'll bring you a pair of earplugs.

when: You have arrived with cash in dollars, euros or yen and need yuan for the small vendors and taxis that still do not scan QR codes.
It is also the question for banks and train stations: exchange counters are rarer than they used to be, so asking at your hotel first saves a wild-goose chase.

variants.en: Is there a bank around here?

mistakes: Changing money at the airport out of caution — the rates there are the worst in the city, and a small first exchange carries you to a bank.
Forgetting your passport: cash exchange is real-name registered in China, and no counter will start the process without it.
Carrying every dollar as cash: once Alipay is set up, cards and QR codes handle nearly everything, and leftover notes mean paying to change them back.

replies.en: Go to the counter, over there.
We need your passport to register it.
We don't take foreign currency today.

when: You are at a licensed exchange counter and want to sanity-check the rate against your banking app before handing over any cash.
The same question works for anyone offering to change money privately — a rate noticeably worse than the app's is the signal to walk away.
mistakes: Comparing against the rate you remember from home — daily moves of one or two percent are normal, so check an app the same morning.
Ignoring the spread: counters show a buying and a selling rate side by side, and the gap between them is where a bad deal hides.
Confusing cash and transfer rates — banknotes exchange at the worse of the two, and the gap between them is bigger than most daily moves.

replies.py: Jīntiān shì yì bǐ qī diǎn èr.
replies.en: Today it's one to seven point two.

replies.zh: 收百分之零点五手续费。

when: Use it at a busy local restaurant where the menu has no photos and no English, and the waiter is already waiting with the order pad.
Also works when friends invite you to eat and the group hands the menu around — volunteering with this sentence saves everyone an awkward pause.

variants.en: I don't know what to order.

mistakes: Pointing at the menu and saying 此菜 — the word is not used in speech; 点菜 is the fixed verb for ordering, and the waiter fills in the rest.
Adding too many conditions to one breath — say your allergy or spice limit first as its own sentence (我不吃海鲜), then hand over the ordering, so nothing gets lost.
Skipping the budget hint — two or three dishes can mean lunch or a banquet; adding 一个人吃 (eating alone) or pointing at a price range keeps the pick sensible.

replies.en: Then I'll sort it out for you.

when: Use it in a restaurant when you want hot water instead of cold drinks, or in a hotel when refilling your bottle before a day out.
It is also the natural follow-up after the waiter pours you something iced and your stomach disagrees.

variants.py: Kěyǐ lái hú rè shuǐ ma?
variants.en: Could we get a kettle of hot water?

mistakes: Saying 水 alone and expecting hot — plain water arrives cold or room-temperature in most restaurants; the word 热 is what carries your request.
Confusing 热水 with 开水 in the wrong direction — 开水 means freshly boiled (hotter, for tea or sterilizing); 热水 is the drinkable hot water you want at the table.
Bringing a closed bottle to the table instead of asking — in a sit-down restaurant hot water is free, so the staff would rather pour it than watch you pay for bottled water.

replies.en: Yes, I'll bring it right away.
Let me pour you hot water.

replies.py: Rè shuǐ hú zài zhuō shàng.
replies.en: The kettle is on the table.

when: Use it while ordering anything braised, soupy or home-style, where salt is the main seasoning and Chinese kitchens season generously by local standard.
Also the right sentence for kids' meals and for anyone managing blood pressure on a long trip.

variants.py: Bú yào tài xián yě bú yào tài yóu.
variants.en: Not too salty and not too oily.

mistakes: Saying it after the dish lands — unlike steak culture, Chinese kitchens rarely re-season mid-service; salt requests only work at ordering time.
Confusing 咸 (salty) with 淡 (bland) — mixing them up requests the exact opposite, so double-check which side of the scale you are on.
Assuming broth-based dishes are safe by default — soups and noodle broths are often the saltiest items on the menu, so the request applies there most of all.

replies.py: Hǎo, ràng chúfáng shǎo fàng yán.
replies.en: Okay, I'll have the kitchen use less salt.

when: Use it in a taxi or didi ride when the driving feels genuinely unsafe — mountain roads, high-speed highway weaving, or rain-slicked streets at night.
Also the calm way to react to a driver racing to beat lights, before it becomes an argument.
mistakes: Shouting 慢点 with an angry tone — the word 请 and a calm voice keep it a request; drivers respond to respect and ignore lectures.
Saying 开车慢点 to a didi app driver before the ride — the sentence belongs mid-ride; before pickup it reads as a complaint about nothing.
Grabbing the seat or door while saying it — physical alarm reads as panic, and the driver will talk to your words, not your hands.

replies.en: Sorry, I'll be careful right away.

replies.zh: 前面路滑，我小点声…不是，小点油门。
replies.py: Qiánmiàn lù huá, wǒ xiǎo diǎn yóumén.
replies.en: Road's slippery ahead — I'll ease off the accelerator.

when: Use it on any ride where you might doze off or get absorbed in your phone — long-distance buses, airport shuttles, night trains, or a didi heading to a station you do not know.
It is also worth saying when you cannot read the stop announcements at all.

variants.en: Give me a shout when we arrive.
Please remind me at the stop.
Please trouble yourself to call me when we get there.

mistakes: Waiting until you are already half-asleep — say it when you board or right after paying, while the driver still has you in working memory.
Pointing at a stop on a map as your only instruction — the sentence needs a destination already agreed (the address card or a named stop); it reminds, it does not define.
Saying it to nobody in particular on a big bus — aim it at the driver or conductor; on trains with conductors, 叫 works better than hoping for a PA announcement.

replies.py: Hǎo, dào le wǒ jiào nǐ.
replies.en: Sure, I'll call you when we arrive.

when: Use it at the hotel front desk on check-in evening, when jet lag makes a 6 a.m. departure or an early tour real.
Also the backup for a phone alarm you do not trust on the first morning in a new time zone.

variants.zh: 请明天早上六点半叫我起床。
variants.py: Qǐng míngtiān zǎoshang liù diǎn bàn jiào wǒ qǐchuáng.
variants.en: Please wake me at 6:30 tomorrow morning.
Set up a morning call for me.

mistakes: Saying the sentence without a time and walking away — wake-up calls are always logged with an hour; without one the desk either asks again or does nothing.
Confusing 叫醒 (wake up) with 叫 (call) alone — 叫我 alone can mean 'call my room by phone'; 叫醒 is the word that guarantees someone gets you out of bed.
Booking it for 明天 alone — 明天 spans all day, and 早上 or 明早 is the part that makes the desk schedule it before breakfast.

replies.py: Hǎo, míngzǎo qī diǎn jiào nín.
replies.en: Okay, we'll wake you at 7 tomorrow.
The wake-up call is a phone call to your room.

when: Use it at check-in or once you are in the room and find none, since budget hotels often keep hairdryers at the front desk.
Also handy before an early morning when you cannot wait for housekeeping to open.

variants.en: Is there a hairdryer in the room?

variants.py: Kěyǐ jiè yí gè chuīfēngjī ma?

variants.en: Do I pick up a hairdryer at the front desk?

mistakes: Searching the closet in silence before asking — many hotels store hairdryers in drawers, but the front desk answer arrives faster than your second wardrobe check.
Confusing 吹风机 with 风扇 — a fan blows but does not heat; the 吹 character (blow-dry) is the one that means hairdryer.
Forgetting the deposit pattern — some desks lend electrical items against a cash deposit; asking 有吗 first and 借 second handles both cases.

replies.py: Zài qiántái, jiāo yājīn jiù néng ná.
replies.en: At the front desk — leave a deposit and you can take it.
No hairdryer, but there's a fan.

when: Use it in the fitting room or right after trying a jacket over your clothes, when the size is close but one step too loose.
It keeps the sale moving — the seller immediately reaches for a smaller size instead of waiting for you to decide.

variants.py: Tài dà le, yǒu xiǎo yí hào de ma?
variants.en: Too big — do you have one size smaller?

mistakes: Saying 不好看 (ugly) when you mean the fit — keep the judgment on size only; 有点大 gets a size swap, 不好看 ends the conversation.
Confusing 号 (size) with 大 alone — for shoes and clothes, asking for 小一号 (one size smaller) is the sentence sellers actually act on.
Swapping 大 and 小 under pressure — pause one second; this is the single most costly two-character mix-up in a Chinese fitting room.

replies.py: Gěi nǐ huàn xiǎo yí hào.
replies.en: I'll get you one size smaller.

replies.py: Zhè hái yǒu gè xiǎo mǎ de.

when: Use it when checking last entry times at sights, catching the last metro, or syncing with a train departure when your phone is dead or buried.
Also the polite icebreaker before asking 请问… at a bus stop.

variants.en: Excuse me, what time is it now?
What time is it — is there still time?

mistakes: Understanding 点 but missing 半 — 半 means half past, so 五点半 is 5:30, and 差一刻 means a quarter to; these two words cover most real answers.
Asking without 请问 to a stranger — bare 现在几点 is fine among friends but abrupt to someone older; one soft word up front changes the tone completely.
Expecting a 24-hour answer — locals say 下午三点 (3 p.m.) and 早上八点 (8 a.m.); listening for those two words matters more than the number.

when: Use it after a lost passport, a serious incident, or any situation where you need official help from your own country and local staff are your fastest path to a phone line.
It is the formal sentence — hotel desks, police stations and hospitals all recognize it instantly.

variants.zh: 我想联系中国的大使馆。
variants.py: Wǒ xiǎng liánxì Zhōngguó de dàshǐguǎn.
variants.en: I want to contact the embassy in China.

variants.zh: 请帮我联系我的领事馆。
variants.py: Qǐng bāng wǒ liánxì wǒ de lǐngshìguǎn.
variants.en: Please help me contact my consulate.

variants.zh: 我需要大使馆的电话号码。
variants.py: Wǒ xūyào dàshǐguǎn de diànhuà hàomǎ.
variants.en: I need the embassy's phone number.

mistakes: Saying it to taxi drivers on the street — 大使馆 matters to hotel staff and police; a random street ask wastes the sentence's authority.
Confusing 大使馆 (embassy, Beijing) with 领事馆 (consulate, other cities) — either word works, but knowing your city's version saves one explanation round.
Skipping your country's Chinese name — adding 美国 (USA), 英国 (UK) or 澳大利亚 (Australia) after the sentence gets you the right building on the first try.

replies.en: I'll look up the number for you.

replies.zh: 大使馆在北京，领事馆在上海。
replies.py: Dàshǐguǎn zài Běijīng, lǐngshìguǎn zài Shànghǎi.
replies.en: The embassy is in Beijing; the consulate is in Shanghai.
Which country are you a citizen of?

when: Use it at any restaurant, noodle shop or street stall before or while ordering — cilantro comes as a default garnish across most of China.
It is also the right answer to 加不加香菜, the question you will hear constantly in canteens and noodle shops.

variants.en: Put the cilantro on the side.

mistakes: Mixing up 不要辣 and 不要香菜 — 辣 is chili spice and 香菜 is the herb; the wrong one brings you chili oil instead of removing the garnish.
Staying silent and picking it out later — staff garnish dishes automatically, so stating 不要香菜 before cooking keeps it out of the broth entirely.
Forgetting the same pattern for 葱 (scallions) — the other herb sprinkled on nearly as widely, and the identical 不要葱 keeps it off too.

replies.en: The cilantro will come on the side.

when: Use it at restaurants when a dish is going fast and you want another order of the same thing — pointing at the plate removes any doubt about which one.
It works just as well at street stalls and canteens, where portions run small and ordering one more round is completely normal.
mistakes: Using 一杯 for food — 杯 counts drinks and 份 counts dishes; the measure word is what makes the sentence sound native.
Dropping 来 and saying 再一份 — it is understood, but 再来 is the fixed rhythm everyone actually says.
Ordering a second round after the kitchen has stopped — many kitchens close half an hour before the restaurant does, so ask 还能点吗 first.

when: Ask it when you arrive somewhere new — a hotel, a homestay, a station exit — to judge whether you should walk, ride the metro or take a taxi.
It is also the polite way to start a fare estimate with a taxi driver before you get in.

variants.py: Zhèlǐ lí dìtiě zhàn yuǎn ma?
variants.en: Is it far from the metro station?
How far is it from here?
Can I get there on foot?

mistakes: Using 是 to connect two places — Chinese measures distance with A 离 B 远, never A 是 B 远; 离 is the preposition that carries the distance.
Confusing 远 (far) with 久 (a long time) — distance answers in kilometers and time in minutes, and 多远 vs 多久 is what picks between them.
Expecting an exact distance — locals answer with walking time or landmarks, so follow up with 走路要多久 (how long does it take to walk).

replies.en: Not far, ten minutes on foot.
A bit far; I'd suggest the metro.

when: Use it on a platform, at a bus stop or outside a metro gate before you board — confirming the destination costs nothing and saves a wrong-way ride.
Swap the destination and the sentence still works: any 火车站, 市中心 or landmark name fits straight into the slot.

variants.py: Zhè tàng chē dào shìzhōngxīn ma?

variants.zh: 这路公交车去火车站吗？
variants.py: Zhè lù gōngjiāochē qù huǒchēzhàn ma?
variants.en: Does this bus go to the train station?

variants.py: Wǒ gāi zuò jǐ hào xiàn?
variants.en: Which metro line should I take?

mistakes: Saying 这车 without 趟 — 趟 is the measure word for a scheduled run, and 这趟车 is the fixed phrase staff expect to hear.
Dropping the 吗 — 这趟车去机场 without it is a statement, not a question, and staff may just nod along without correcting you.
Asking after the doors have opened — drivers on express routes may not wait, so confirm before you step in rather than once you are on.

replies.en: Yes, it goes to the airport.

replies.py: Bú qù, nǐ zuò fǎn le.
replies.en: It doesn't; you're headed the wrong way.

replies.py: Zhè tàng bú qù, xià yí tàng qù.
replies.en: This one doesn't; the next one does.

when: Use it at a hotel front desk, a restaurant counter or any staffed reception when you want someone else to handle the calling — it is the standard polite way to get a cab.
It also works in shops and malls, where staff can summon a car on an app for you when the street outside is busy.

variants.py: Kěyǐ bāng wǒ jiào ge chē ma?
variants.en: Can you call me a car?

variants.py: Qǐng bāng wǒ yòng Dīdī jiào chē.
variants.en: Please call me a car with Didi.

variants.zh: 麻烦帮我叫出租车，去机场。
variants.py: Máfan bāng wǒ jiào chūzūchē, qù jīchǎng.
variants.en: Please call me a taxi — I'm going to the airport.

mistakes: Saying 打车 when you want someone else to do it — 打车 is what you do yourself; the key words in this sentence are 帮我 (for me).
Hailing from the curb at rush hour — in big cities most cars are dispatched by app, and a front desk 叫车 beats waving your arm.
Forgetting to say where you are going — adding 去机场 or an address while asking gets the right kind of car the first time.

replies.en: Sure, I'll call one for you.

replies.py: Nín shāo děng, wǔ fēnzhōng dào.
replies.en: Wait a moment; it will arrive in five minutes.

when: Use it at the front desk when the door reader refuses your card — a dead card is routine, and this sentence gets it fixed without any embarrassment.
It also covers the checkout-day case: the card expired at noon and you still need to step back inside for your bags.

variants.en: I can't get into my room.

mistakes: Keeping the card in your phone case or against a magnet — this is the top cause of dead cards, and staff guess it the moment they hear the sentence.
Describing the problem but leaving the card in the room — bring the card itself to the front desk; they recharge or re-encode it in seconds.
Panicking after noon — cards stop at checkout time by design, and the desk reactivates yours if a late checkout was agreed.

replies.py: Wǒ gěi nín chóngxīn zuò yì zhāng.
replies.en: I'll make you a new one.

replies.zh: 是不是跟手机放一起了？
replies.py: Shì bu shì gēn shǒujī fàng yìqǐ le?
replies.en: Was it next to your phone?

when: Use it inside a bank, or when asking staff where the ATM is — 取钱 (withdraw money) is the everyday word, and tellers hear it from everyone.
It also works at a bank counter with your passport and card, where staff will route you to a foreign-card machine or a human teller.

variants.en: I would like to withdraw five hundred yuan.

variants.py: Wǒ de kǎ qǔ bu liǎo qián.

mistakes: Mixing up 取钱 (withdraw) and 存钱 (deposit) — the words look alike on screen, and pressing 存款 feeds money in instead of taking it out.
Using convenience-store ATMs with a foreign card — stick to big banks like 中国银行 and 工商银行, whose machines take international cards with an English menu.
Withdrawing small amounts repeatedly — foreign cards usually cap daily amounts and every withdrawal carries a fee, so take what you need in one go.

replies.en: Please use the ATM over there.
The daily withdrawal limit is two thousand yuan.

when: Use it when directions, prices or instructions finally click — it closes the loop politely and encourages people to keep talking with you.
Say it instead of nodding silently after someone re-explains something slowly; the phrase tells them their effort worked.
mistakes: Confusing 明白 with 知道 — 明白 means the explanation made sense, 知道 means you know the fact; after an explanation, 明白了 is the natural reply.
Saying it when you actually don't understand — politeness stops the explanation exactly when you need it most, and 我不太明白 keeps it going.
Dropping the 了 — 我明白 alone sounds like a general claim about your abilities; 了 marks that the understanding just happened.

replies.py: Bù míngbai de huà zài wèn wǒ.
replies.en: If it is not clear, ask me again.

replies.py: Wǒ zài gěi nǐ jiǎng yí biàn.
replies.en: Let me explain it once more.

when: Use it at a pharmacy counter or clinic — stomach trouble is the number-one traveler complaint in China, and this sentence gets you medicine fast.
It also works in a taxi heading to a hospital, and with hotel staff who can point you to the nearest pharmacy or doctor.
mistakes: Saying 胃疼 when you are not sure which organ it is — 肚子 (belly) covers everything between chest and hips and is what pharmacists expect first.
Dropping the body part and saying 我疼 — Chinese names the spot; 疼 alone sounds vague even to a doctor.
Toughing it out for days — pharmacies sell effective stomach medicine over the counter, and staff can route you the moment they hear 肚子疼.

replies.en: I suggest going to the hospital for a check.

when: Use it at the airport lost-luggage desk first, then at your hotel front desk if the airline sent your bag on later — both places act on it immediately.
It also works at train stations, where left-behind or mixed-up bags end up at the station's lost and found.

variants.zh: 行李转盘上没有我的箱子。
variants.py: Xíngli zhuànpán shàng méiyǒu wǒ de xiāngzi.
variants.en: My suitcase isn't on the carousel.

mistakes: Going to the airline counter instead of 行李查询 — at Chinese airports the lost-luggage desk next to the carousel is the correct first stop.
Throwing away the baggage tag — the sticky stub links the search to your bag, so keep it until the bag is back in your hands.
Confusing 丢 with 偷 — 丢 starts a search for a lost bag, while 被偷 (stolen) turns it into a police matter with a different response.

replies.en: Do you have the baggage tag?

replies.py: Qǐng miáoshù yíxià nín de xiāngzi.
Bié jí, wǒmen bāng nín zhǎo.
replies.en: Don't worry; we will help you find it.

when: Ask it only where foreign currency plausibly works — border towns, big tourist hotels, airline offices — because most everyday shops in China take yuan only.
It is also the honest way to check before pulling out cash that may be useless, so you learn the answer before the transaction starts.

variants.en: Can I pay in US dollars?
Can I change US dollars here?

mistakes: Assuming big cities mean broad acceptance — even in Shanghai or Beijing, street shops and taxis take yuan or QR payment, and dollars only work in a handful of counters.
Confusing 美金 with 美元 — both mean US dollars and both are understood, but 美金 is the spoken word people use and 美元 leans written.
Offering large notes in a small shop — even where dollars are taken, change comes back in yuan, so keep small bills and expect the rate to include a margin.

replies.en: You can change it at the bank over there.

when: Ask it before any money service — changing cash at a bank or exchange counter, withdrawing at an ATM with a foreign card, or wiring money — because the fee is often not shown until you commit.
It also works for ticket changes and hotel deposits: any time an extra charge might be hiding, this is the question that surfaces it.

variants.en: Is there a fee for withdrawing money?
What is the fee for changing money?
How much of a fee do you charge?

mistakes: Only comparing the headline exchange rate — a great rate with a heavy commission can lose to a fair rate with no fee, which is why the question comes before the transaction.
Skipping the question at ATMs — foreign-card withdrawals can carry two fees, one from each bank, and neither may appear on screen before you accept.
Confusing 手续费 with 小费 — 手续费 is the service fee you cannot avoid; 小费 is a tip, and tipping is not expected anywhere in China.

when: Ask it when a purchase is bulky or fragile — teapots, paintings, ceramics — and you would rather have it arrive home than survive your suitcase.
It also opens the shipping conversation early: if the shop cannot send abroad, they may point you to a forwarding service, and you learn that before you pay.

variants.en: Can you ship to the United States?

variants.py: Kěyǐ bāng wǒ jì kuàidì ma?
variants.en: Can you help me send this by courier?
Roughly how much is the shipping?

mistakes: Asking at markets and small stalls — international shipping lives at big shops, galleries and malls; a stall's answer will be no and the sentence works better one level up.
Forgetting that 快递 is the magic word — domestic couriers are everywhere and cheap, so a nearby 快递点 can ship for you even when the shop itself cannot.
Packing before asking — shops that do ship abroad pack to survive the trip, and their materials are better than what you have; ask first, let them wrap it.

replies.py: Yào tián yì zhāng kuàidì dān.
replies.en: You'll need to fill in a courier form.

when: Use it when you genuinely want two or more of something — a second item in hand is the strongest bargaining chip a market seller will see all day.
It also works in small shops with a little flexibility, though in fixed-price chain stores the answer is a polite no and nothing is lost by asking.

variants.py: Mǎi sān gè néng piányi diǎn ma?
variants.en: Any discount if I buy three?

variants.py: Duō mǎi jǐ gè néng dǎzhé ma?
variants.en: If I buy several, is there a discount?

mistakes: Promising to buy more and then buying one — sellers remember, and the discount you talk them into is real money out of their pocket; only ask if you mean it.
Asking before checking the item — agree on quality and size first, because the discount conversation makes no sense if the thing doesn't fit.
Using 个 for clothes — 件 is the measure word for garments and 个 is for objects; 买两个T恤 sounds off, 买两件 is the natural line.

replies.py: Liǎng jiàn gěi nǐ suàn yìbǎi.
replies.en: Two for a hundred, I'll count it for you.

replies.py: Mǎi liǎng jiàn sòng yì shuāng wàzi.
replies.en: Buy two and I'll throw in a pair of socks.

replies.py: Yí jiàn jiùshì yí jiàn de jià.

when: Use it at the station's ticket window as soon as plans change — train tickets refund for a fee that grows as departure approaches, so early is cheap and late is expensive.
It also covers flights and long-distance buses, though each carrier has its own cutoff and the counter staff will state it once you say the line.

variants.py: Zhè zhāng piào néng tuì ma?

variants.en: Can I change it to tomorrow?
How much do they deduct for a refund?

mistakes: Going to the automatic machines — refunds and changes happen at the staffed window (人工窗口) with the passport you booked under, so machines are not the door for this one.
Waiting until after departure — missed trains have their own same-day rules that are stricter than a refund before departure, so walk to the window the moment the plan breaks.
Confusing 退票 with 改签 — 退票 returns the money, 改签 moves you to another train; often 改签 costs less, so ask for both prices.

replies.py: Shōu bǎifēn zhī wǔ de shǒuxùfèi.

replies.zh: 开车前两小时以内不行。
replies.py: Kāichē qián liǎng xiǎoshí yǐnèi bù xíng.
replies.en: Not within two hours of departure.
Please show your passport and the ticket.

when: Use it the moment you realise the bus or metro has carried you past your stop — on the metro the fix is automatic (ride back one stop), on a bus you need the driver to hear it now.
It also works in taxis when you spot the landmark flying by, though there you are more likely to say 请在前面停车 instead.

variants.py: Zuò guò zhàn le, zěnme bàn?
variants.en: I missed my stop — what do I do?

mistakes: Rushing off at the next stop to walk back — on the metro the same line carries you back for free, and on a bus the next stop may be a motorway ramp; staying aboard is usually the better move.
Confusing 坐过站 with 坐错车 — 过站 means the right vehicle went one stop too far; 错车 means the wrong line entirely, and the fix for those is very different.
Waiting for the announcement in English — smaller cities and buses announce in Chinese only, so watch the stops on a map app as you ride.

replies.py: Xià yí zhàn xiàchē zài zuò huílái.
replies.en: Get off at the next stop and ride back.

replies.py: Xiànzài bù néng tíng, dào zhàn cái xíng.
replies.en: I can't stop now — only at a stop.
No worries — it's just one stop over.

when: Use it at any stop, pier or station where runs are scheduled — buses, ferries, airport shuttles — and the timetable on the wall is either absent or in Chinese only.
It also works for the last service of the night: pair it with 末班车是几点 (what time is the last one) before you commit to dinner across town.

variants.en: What time is the last one?

variants.py: Zhè tàng chē hái yǒu ma?

mistakes: Using 次 instead of 班 for transit — 班 is the measure word for scheduled runs, so 下一班几点 is the fixed phrase; 次 belongs to counting times something happens.
Asking 你 instead of the schedule — drivers on break and queue staff know the line by heart, and the answer is usually faster than digging out your phone.
Not confirming the direction — the same route number often runs two ways from nearby stops, so add 到XX的方向 (the direction toward X) if the stop serves both.

replies.py: Gāng zǒu le yì bān, zài děng děng.
replies.en: One just left — wait a bit.
The last one is at nine thirty.

when: Use it at the front desk the night before your checkout day — rooms from booking apps are commonly released for resale in the morning, so the evening ask is the one that succeeds.
It also fits the shorter ask for a late room on the same day, though that version is usually 我可以晚点退房 and handled as a checkout extension instead.

variants.py: Kěyǐ zài zhù yì wǎn ma?
variants.en: Can I stay one more night?
Could I extend by two days?
Do you still have rooms tomorrow?

mistakes: Asking on checkout morning — the room may already be sold through the app by then, and the clerk genuinely cannot undo it; the night before is the reliable moment.
Expecting the same rate — walk-in extension prices can differ from your booking app, so ask the price with the room and decide with the number in hand.
Forgetting the room change — extensions sometimes move you to another room, which means packing; ask 换房间吗 (am I changing rooms?) before you say yes.

replies.py: Kěyǐ, jiā yì wǎn sānbāi bā.
replies.en: Yes — one more night is 380 yuan.

replies.py: Míngwǎn yǒu fáng, yào huàn fángjiān.
replies.en: There's a room tomorrow, but you'd change rooms.

replies.zh: 您在系统里重新订一下。
replies.py: Nín zài xìtǒng lǐ chóngxīn dìng yíxià.

when: Use it to agree to any request — a server suggesting a table, a driver offering a detour, a stranger asking you to hold a place in line — it is the friendly yes that keeps the exchange moving.
It also answers a thank-you: say it with a wave after 谢谢 and it reads as 'don't mention it', the local equivalent of 'no problem at all'.

variants.en: No problem — leave it to me.

mistakes: Confusing 没问题 with 没关系 — 没问题 agrees to a request; 没关系 forgives a mistake, and swapping them makes you accept apologies you meant to wave off.
Using it to answer a request you cannot actually do — the phrase is a real commitment here, so check feasibility first and fall back on 我试试 (let me try) when unsure.
Saying it flatly with a straight face — the phrase carries warmth, and with a smile it lands as easygoing rather than grudging.

replies.py: Xièxie, nà jiù bàituō nǐ le.
replies.en: Thanks — I'll leave it in your hands.

when: Use it at any information desk, station office or police post the moment you lose your group in a crowd — staff handle this daily and will usually broadcast or call for you.
It also works on the phone to the missing friend: the sentence tells whoever answers where you are calling from and that you are staying put.

variants.py: Wǒ zhǎo bu dào wǒ péngyou le.

variants.zh: 我们走散了，能广播一下吗？
variants.py: Wǒmen zǒusàn le, néng guǎngbō yíxià ma?
variants.en: We got separated — could you make an announcement?

mistakes: Roaming while searching — pick a fixed landmark and stay there, because a moving person is the one thing both searchers cannot find; staff will tell you the same thing.
Saving this for later — the moment you cannot see them and they cannot see you, ask staff; ten minutes of searching alone in a crowd is how minutes become hours.
Forgetting the screenshot — a photo of the person on your phone is what an announcement or a police report actually needs, and it is the fastest way to describe them.

replies.py: Bié zǒu, wǒ bāng nín guǎngbō.
replies.en: Stay here — I'll make an announcement.
Do you have a photo of them?

when: Use it the moment the waiter asks anything about spice — it is the safest answer when 只有一点辣 sounds risky but 不要辣 feels like a shame at a good noodle shop.
It also works when ordering for the table: say it for the whole dish so the kitchen sets the heat level once instead of scattering requests.

variants.en: Even a tiny bit of spice is okay.

mistakes: Saying 不要辣 when you actually want 微辣 — kitchens take it literally and you get zero chili; 微辣 is a distinct setting, not a weaker version of no spice.
Assuming 微辣 is mild by your home standard — in Sichuan or Hunan their mild can still bite, so keep 请给我水 ready.
Forgetting the word order — it is 微辣就行, not 就行微辣; the spice level always comes first, 就行 closes the sentence.

replies.zh: 我们家的微辣有点辣，没问题吧？
replies.py: Wǒmen jiā de wēi là yǒudiǎn là, méi wèntí ba?
replies.en: Our mild is a bit spicy — still okay?

replies.py: Yào wánquán bú fàng là ma?
replies.en: Do you want no chili at all?

when: Ask it at the door of any busy restaurant, ticket window or food stall when the queue in front of you is long and you need to decide whether to wait.
Use it with a queue number in hand too — if the answer is over half an hour, 多少号 now means a walk and a return, and this question tells you which.

variants.en: How much longer is the wait?

variants.py: Xiànzài pái dào jǐ hào le?
variants.en: Which number are they on now?

mistakes: Dropping 要 — 要等多久 is the natural question; 等多久 alone sounds clipped and 多久等 doesn't work at all.
Mishearing 分钟 as 点钟 — 二十分钟 means twenty minutes; 二十点 would mean eight o'clock, a completely different answer.
Walking away without a queue number — many places won't call you if you never took one; combine with a photo of the ticket so you remember your 号.

replies.en: There are three tables ahead of you.

replies.zh: 人多的时候要等一小时。
replies.py: Rén duō de shíhou yào děng yì xiǎoshí.
replies.en: At busy times you wait an hour.

when: Use it on the platform or inside the train when signs are crowded with numbers and you need to confirm the car you boarded is the line you meant.
It also works at transfer stations — before you follow the crowd down the corridor, confirm the next platform is the line your map shows.

variants.py: Zhè shì èr hào xiàn ma?
Qù XX zuò jǐ hào xiàn?

mistakes: Saying 几线 instead of 几号线 — the 号 belongs inside the question; 几号线 is the fixed phrase staff expect.
Confusing the line number with the exit number — 2号线 is the metro line, 2号口 is exit 2; mixing them sends you to the wrong surface.
Not checking direction — Chinese lines name their terminus, so confirm 往 (bound for) plus the last stop, not just the line number.

replies.zh: 这是 10 号线，往虹桥火车站方向。
replies.py: Zhè shì shí hào xiàn, wǎng Hóngqiáo Huǒchēzhàn fāngxiàng.
replies.en: This is Line 10, bound for Hongqiao Railway Station.

replies.py: Duìmiàn jiù shì èr hào xiàn.
replies.en: Line 2 is right across the platform.

when: Use it when you land somewhere new and need water, a charger, snacks or an ATM at odd hours — convenience stores are the one thing China's streets never run out of.
Ask it before you leave a hotel or metro station at night; the answer plus a direction pointing keeps the walk short and safe.

variants.en: Where is the nearest convenience store?
What time does the convenience store close?

mistakes: Calling it 方便店 — the store is 便利店 (convenience store); 方便 belongs to 方便面 (instant noodles) and polite questions.
Expecting a 7-Eleven everywhere — coverage differs by city; 罗森, 全家 and 便利蜂 are the names you will actually see.
Forgetting you can pay by cash there too — if Alipay fails, convenience stores are the classic fallback for 支付宝没绑好 moments.

replies.py: Qiánmiàn lùkǒu jiù yǒu yì jiā.
replies.en: There's one at the intersection ahead.

replies.py: Chū jiǔdiàn wǎng zuǒ, wǔshí mǐ.
replies.en: Exit the hotel, turn left, 50 meters.

replies.zh: 对面那家 24 小时开门。
replies.py: Duìmiàn nà jiā èrshísì xiǎoshí kāimén.
replies.en: The one across the street is open 24 hours.

when: Use it at the front desk or over the room phone when your room needs freshening up mid-stay and no one has come by.
It also works on checkout morning when you are packing and want the room tidied before you return to collect luggage.

variants.py: Kěyǐ bāng wǒ qīnglǐ yíxià ma?
variants.en: Can you clean it up for me?
What time can it be cleaned?

variants.py: Néng duō ná liǎng píng shuǐ ma?
variants.en: Could you bring two more bottles of water?

mistakes: Using 洗 instead of 打扫 — 洗房间 sounds like washing; 打扫 is the verb housekeeping actually answers to.
Blocking the door tag — if you hang 请勿打扰 (do not disturb), staff skip your room all day; take it down before going out.
Leaving valuables in the open — cleaning staff are trustworthy but tipping cash on the desk can vanish into the tidy-up; pocket it first.

replies.py: Hǎo de, xiàwǔ liǎng diǎn qián dǎsǎo.
replies.en: Sure, it will be cleaned before 2pm.

replies.py: Nín bǎ ménpái guà fǎn le jiù xíng.
replies.en: Just flip the door tag over.
Is now a good time to come in?

when: Report it at the front desk or call reception when the shower or tap runs cold no matter how long you wait — winter hotels can genuinely run out on busy nights.
Use it before you shower, not after: test the water first, and if this comes out of your mouth dripping wet, the towel situation becomes urgent too.

variants.en: The hot water has run out.

mistakes: Saying 没水 when the problem is only temperature — 没水 means no water at all; 没有热水 points the repair at the right pipe.
Not testing both taps — hot is labelled 热水, cold 冷水; tourists sometimes twist the wrong handle and blame the boiler.
Only texting the booking app — reception fixes it in minutes; an app message may reach nobody until morning.

replies.py: Wǒmen mǎshàng pài rén lái xiū.
replies.en: We'll send someone to fix it right away.
Wait ten minutes and try again.

replies.py: Gěi nín huàn yì jiān fáng.
replies.en: We'll move you to another room.

when: Ask it before paying for any hotel rate, tour or train ticket when plans might change — many cheap Chinese rates are 不退不改, no refund and no change.
Use it on booking apps too: the filter 免费取消 uses exactly these words, so asking it in person or reading it on screen is the same check.

variants.en: What's the latest I can cancel?

mistakes: Assuming 24-hour rules like home platforms — many Chinese hotel rates lock at booking, so ask before you tap pay, not after.
Confusing 取消 with 退票 — 取消 kills a future booking; 退票 refunds an issued ticket; both appear on the same app page and mean different money.
Cancelling by not showing up — no-shows often forfeit the first night; a real cancellation call protects the wallet.

replies.zh: 可以，入住当天下午六点前都行。
replies.py: Kěyǐ, rùzhù dàngtiān xiàwǔ liù diǎn qián dōu xíng.
replies.en: Yes, anytime before 6pm on check-in day.
Cancelling costs one night's room fee.

when: Use it when you fall for something bulky — a suitcase, a tea set, ceramics — and cannot face carrying it through the metro at rush hour.
It also works when you are checking out tomorrow and shipping straight home is easier: the shop can send it to the hotel to repack, or onward.

variants.en: Can you help me send it by courier?
Can you send it to the airport?
