mistakes: Leaving only the English hotel name — couriers need the Chinese address; screenshot it from the booking app before you shop.
Forgetting your checkout date — say 我明天退房 (I check out tomorrow) so it arrives before you, not after.
Paying without a receipt for the courier — the 取件码 (pickup code) or tracking number on it is how you chase the parcel.

replies.py: Nín bǎ jiǔdiàn dìzhǐ gěi wǒ.

replies.en: That's ten yuan extra for shipping.

when: Say it at the scene of a fall, cut or sprain — it tells bystanders instantly that this is an injury needing action, not just confusion.
Use it at the hospital or pharmacy too: it opens the visit faster than describing the story, and then you point or name the body part.
mistakes: Saying 我疼了 — Chinese uses 疼 as a statement like 腿疼 (my leg hurts); 受伤 is the word for injured and what triggers real help.
Understating to be polite — Chinese strangers will take 疼 as minor; 流血了 (it's bleeding) or 骨头可能断了 (a bone may be broken) gets you an ambulance, not a band-aid.
Waiting to find exact words — 120 is the national emergency medical number; call it, then use this phrase on the phone.

replies.en: I'll help you to the hospital.

when: Use it in taxis and DiDi cars in summer when the driver has windows down and AC off — fuel-saving habit, and this sentence is the polite nudge.
It works for hotel rooms and restaurants too: any time 空调 is switched off and the room is turning into a steam room, ask it before you sweat through your shirt.

variants.zh: 可以把空调开大一点吗？
variants.py: Kěyǐ bǎ kōngtiáo kāi dà yìdiǎn ma?
variants.en: Can you turn the AC up?

variants.py: Tài rè le, néng kāi kōngtiáo ma?
variants.en: It's too hot — can you turn on the AC?

mistakes: Saying 开空调吗 when you want it colder in a cooled room — 开 is on/off; 开大一点 (turn it up) or 调低一点 (turn the temperature down) is the follow-up you actually need.
Mixing up 开 and 关 — 关空调 turns it off; getting this wrong in winter makes a cold taxi even colder.
Skipping 太热了 as a softener — adding the reason first makes the request friendly, and drivers respond to warmth better than commands.

replies.zh: 空调坏了，您介意开窗吗？
replies.py: Kōngtiáo huài le, nín jièyì kāi chuāng ma?
replies.en: The AC is broken — mind if we open the windows?
What temperature shall I set it to?

when: Say it the moment you step into a busy restaurant with no host stand — the nearest staff member will either wave you to a table or start a waitlist with your name.
It also works at the door of a full noodle shop at lunch rush: asking takes two seconds and often gets you 两位马上 (two seats right away) instead of standing around guessing.

variants.py: Yǒu liǎng wèi de wèizi ma?
variants.en: Is there a table for two?

mistakes: Using 房间 (room) or 位置 for a restaurant table — 位子 is the natural word for a seat in a restaurant; 位置 means a location or position and sounds like you're asking about the building.
Skipping the party size — 有位子吗 gets you moving, but adding 两位 or 三位 up front lets the staff match you to the right table in one step instead of a second round of gestures.
Waiting outside a half-empty restaurant — in many casual places you seat yourself; if nobody responds to 有位子吗, walk toward any open table and the staff will stop you if it's reserved.

replies.en: Wait a moment, it'll be ready soon.

when: Use it when the table has no chopsticks — common in hotel breakfast rooms, Western-style cafés, or when a box of them sits out of reach on a shared shelf.
It also works mid-meal when yours fell on the floor: just catch the staff's eye and say it, they'll bring a fresh pair without a second question.
mistakes: Saying 一个筷子 — chopsticks count as pairs: 一双筷子 (one pair). 一个筷子 makes waiters pause because it literally means one single stick.
Expecting a napkin to come automatically — many places only give tissues in a box on the table, so ask 纸巾 (napkins) the same way when you need them.
Waiting silently at fancy restaurants — high-end places set forks by default; if you want to eat Chinese-style there, you have to ask, nobody will guess.

replies.zh: 筷子在那边的抽屉里，自己拿。
replies.py: Kuàizi zài nàbiān de chōuti li, zìjǐ ná.
replies.en: Chopsticks are in the drawer over there, help yourself.
Do you need a spoon too?

when: Say it when a waiter suggests another dish, tops up your rice, or asks 还吃吗 (still eating?) — it politely closes the meal so they stop offering.
It also works when a host keeps piling food on your plate at a family-style dinner: this is the gentle, culturally standard way to refuse more without offending anyone.
mistakes: Confusing 饱 with 饿 — 饱 means full, 饿 means hungry; they sound nothing alike but both end sentences about eating, so double-check before you say one.
Saying it too early — hosts hear 我吃饱了 as I'm done, and staff may start clearing the table; use it only when you really are finished.
Forgetting that refusal needs a reason to sound soft — adding 真的 (really) as in 我真的吃饱了 makes it warm instead of curt.

replies.py: Hǎo de, nà gěi nín shàng guǒpán.
replies.en: Okay, then we'll bring the fruit plate.

replies.py: Zhēn bù chī la? Zài lái yìdiǎndiǎn.
replies.en: Really no more? Just a tiny bit more.

replies.zh: 好的，需要打包剩下的吗？
replies.py: Hǎo de, xūyào dǎbāo shèngxià de ma?
replies.en: Okay, do you want to take the leftovers to go?

when: Say it in a train station when you can't match your ticket to the signs — staff at the entrance or security check will point you to the right waiting hall and gate number.
It also works at airports when the Chinese sign 登机口 isn't obvious: show your boarding pass while asking and they'll read the gate for you.

variants.py: Wǒ de jiǎnpiàokǒu shì jǐ hào?

variants.en: Which floor is the waiting area on?

mistakes: Walking to the platform without checking — high-speed rail checks tickets at a specific gate that only opens 10–15 minutes before departure, so find the gate first, not the track.
Ignoring the stop announcement — at big stations the gate number on your ticket changes last-minute; the boards above the waiting hall are the only reliable source.
Using 卖票口 (ticket office window) instead of 检票口 (gate) — they sound similar and both end in 口, but one sells tickets and the other checks them.

replies.py: Kàn dà píngmù, wǎng zuǒbiān zǒu.
replies.en: Check the big screen, go left.

replies.py: Hái yǒu shí fēnzhōng kāishǐ jiǎnpiào.
replies.en: Ticket check starts in ten minutes.

when: Say it when someone is sitting in your assigned seat on a train — show your ticket or the 12306 screen at the same time, and the misunderstanding clears in seconds.
It also works the other way: if you realize you're in the wrong seat, apologize with 对不起 and this sentence explains you're about to move — 我坐错了 (I sat in the wrong seat) is its natural partner.

variants.zh: 不好意思，我坐错位子了。
variants.py: Bù hǎoyìsi, wǒ zuò cuò wèizi le.
variants.en: Sorry, I sat in the wrong seat.

mistakes: Just staring or tapping the person — a quiet point feels rude in a packed carriage; one friendly sentence with the ticket in hand turns an awkward moment into a normal one.
Arguing over a standing seat — on tickets marked 无座 (no seat), standing cars are first-come, and someone with an assigned ticket always wins the seat.
Mixing up 座位 and 位子 — both mean seat and both are fine, but 座位 is the word on tickets and screens, so it's the safest to match with what you're pointing at.

replies.py: Ò duìbùqǐ, wǒ kàn cuò le.

replies.en: No problem, I'll move right away.

replies.py: Nǐ de shì kào chuāng de zhège.
replies.en: Yours is this one by the window.

when: Say it when checking in late, rebooking a hotel, or explaining to a taxi queue why you just walked out of the airport hours behind schedule.
It also works at the airline counter: pairing it with 我要改签 (I want to rebook) gets the conversation moving — the board already shows 延误, but saying it out loud marks you as someone to help.

variants.en: What time can it take off?

mistakes: Assuming the gate staff rebook you — for real delays the airline counter (航空公司柜台) handles changes; the gate crew only boards whoever the new time says.
Mixing 延误 (delayed) with 取消 (cancelled) — the boards distinguish them clearly and so should you: delayed means wait, cancelled means go rebook or refund.
Leaving the airport without a plan — if the delay runs past midnight, many nearby hotels offer free shuttles; ask the information desk instead of paying a surprise taxi fare.

replies.en: You can rebook at the counter.
You can claim a meal voucher.

when: Say it at check-in the night before, together with asking what time breakfast starts — one question gets you the floor, the room name and whether you need a voucher.
It also works the next morning when you're standing in a lobby corridor with no sign in English: any staff member passing by can point you down the right hallway.

variants.en: How do I use the breakfast voucher?
Until what time is breakfast served?

mistakes: Assuming breakfast is included — many Chinese budget chains charge for it separately; if the voucher talk never happened, 早餐在哪里吃 will quickly reveal whether you're paying.
Sleeping past the window — hotel breakfast usually ends at 9:30 or 10:00 sharp, earlier than most Western hotels, so ask the closing time in the same breath.
Looking only for a restaurant sign — some chains serve breakfast in a side shop next door; the voucher or a staff pointer is the only reliable map.

replies.py: Èr lóu, bā diǎn dào jiǔ diǎn bàn.

replies.zh: 凭早餐券去旁边那家店。
replies.py: Píng zǎocānquàn qù pángbiān nà jiā diàn.
replies.en: Use the voucher at the shop next door.

replies.py: Ná fángkǎ dēngjì yíxià jiù xíng.
replies.en: Just register with your room card.

when: Say it before paying when you're unsure about a size — malls and brand stores answer yes and explain the window; market stalls will say no, which is exactly what you want to know before money changes hands.
It also works after the purchase if the tag is still on: bring the receipt (发票 or 小票) and this line opens the exchange desk conversation.

variants.en: Can I return it if it doesn't fit?

variants.py: Wǒ xiǎng huàn gè zhōng hào.
variants.en: I'd like to exchange it for a medium.
Do I need the receipt to exchange?

mistakes: Using 退 (refund) when you mean 换 (exchange) — a refund asks for money back and gets refused far more often; an exchange for another size is an easier yes.
Cutting the tags off first — exchanges almost always require the original tags attached, so wear it once at home with tags folded away, not removed.
Losing the receipt — no 小票 or 发票, no exchange, even in big malls; photograph it the moment you get it.

replies.zh: 七天之内凭小票可以换。
replies.py: Qī tiān zhī nèi píng xiǎopiào kěyǐ huàn.
replies.en: Within seven days, with the receipt, you can exchange.

replies.zh: 标签剪掉了就不能换了。
replies.py: Biāoqiān jiǎn diào le jiù bù néng huàn le.
replies.en: If the tag is cut off, no exchange.

when: Say it at any counter or market stall when 付款 feels vague — it asks whether QR payment works here, which covers Alipay, WeChat Pay, or whatever app you've set up.
It also works for taxis and street vendors: almost everyone displays a QR code on a piece of plastic, and this question confirms yours will be accepted before you fumble for cash.

variants.en: I only have my phone with me.

mistakes: Scanning the wrong code — stalls often show two: one receives payment (收钱码) and one is the vendor's own social QR; the paying one usually says 收款 under it.
Assuming no sign means no QR — many vendors keep the code on a string around their neck or taped inside the cart; ask rather than walking away.
Forgetting your fallback — if the app fails at a critical moment, 我用现金 (I'll use cash) plus small bills still saves the transaction.

replies.en: The code is on that sign.

when: Say it as an opener with taxi drivers, market vendors or anyone chatting you up — it flips the mood instantly: people slow down, smile, and start helping instead of transacting.
It also works as a soft apology before asking something complicated: pair it with 我中文说得不好 and even a mangled question gets full patience.

variants.py: Wǒ dì yī cì lái Shànghǎi.
variants.en: It's my first time in Shanghai.

mistakes: Getting 次 wrong — the measure word for times is 次: 第一次, 第二次, 第三次; using 遍 or 回 here sounds off in this fixed phrase.
Saying it flat like a fact — this line works because of warmth; a smile and a little effort on the tones does more than perfect grammar ever could.
Expecting English back — some will switch to English, many will just speak slower Chinese; either way 请说慢一点 keeps the exchange alive.

replies.en: Which places have you been to?

replies.py: Zhōngguó cài chī de guàn ma?
replies.en: Is the food agreeing with you?
